---
title: "The Limits of Standard Network Meta-Analysis"
---

## Introduction {#sec-limits-intro}

The previous two chapters built the standard machinery of indirect comparison. Bucher's theorem
(@thm-bucher-unbiased) makes the anchored estimator $\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}$ unbiased for the
$A$-versus-$B$ network contrast, and the network meta-analysis of Chapter 15 generalizes the same
subtraction to an arbitrary connected graph of treatments. Every one of those results rests on a single
load-bearing hypothesis: the **constancy of relative effects** (@def-constancy-relative-effects),
equivalently **transitivity** (@def-transitivity), the assumption that the relative effect of one
treatment versus another is the same number in every study population in the network. This chapter is the
study of what happens when that hypothesis is false. It is, in a precise sense, the chapter that the
remainder of the book exists to answer.

Two distinct failures are at work, and the chapter treats them in turn. The first is direct. We saw at
the end of Chapter 14 (@sec-bucher-failure) that an **effect modifier** (@def-effect-modifier) whose
distribution differs across the trial populations breaks transitivity, because the marginal relative
effect a trial reports is then a population-specific average of a varying conditional effect. The
**failure-of-Bucher theorem** of this chapter (@thm-failure-of-bucher) makes that statement quantitative:
it gives the exact asymptotic bias of the unadjusted indirect comparison as an explicit pair of integrals
against the difference of covariate distributions. The bias is not a small-sample artifact; it does not
shrink as the trials grow, it is invisible in the Bucher standard error of @thm-bucher-variance, and it
can be large enough to reverse the sign of the estimated treatment difference.

The second failure is subtler, and it concerns the natural first attempt at a cure. If the trouble is
that an effect modifier is distributed differently across trials, why not regress the trial-level
treatment effects on the trial-level covariate means and read off the modification? This is
**aggregate-level meta-regression**, and the reason it cannot recover the within-patient effect-modifier
coefficient is the **ecological fallacy**. Averaging a nonlinear inverse link over a covariate
distribution is not the same as applying the inverse link to the average covariate; the gap is a Jensen
gap (@thm-jensen), the same nonlinearity that makes the odds ratio and the hazard ratio non-collapsible
(@def-non-collapsibility). We define **ecological bias** precisely (@def-ecological-bias) and prove, with
a closed-form probit computation, that the slope of an aggregate regression is a strictly attenuated
version of the individual-level interaction coefficient (@thm-ecological-norecovery). Aggregate data, in
short, do not contain the information that the correction requires.

The synthesis is the motivation for Part IV. Both failures point to the same two missing ingredients: the
individual-level effect-modifier coefficient, which needs patient-level data from at least one trial to
estimate without ecological bias; and an integration of the individual model over the *target* covariate
distribution, in place of the illegitimate plug-in of a covariate mean. A method that supplies both is a
**population-adjusted indirect comparison**. Matching-adjusted indirect comparison (Chapter 18), the
simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19), and multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20) are
three such methods, and the precise gap this chapter exhibits is exactly what they are built to close.

Throughout we keep the notation of [Notation](/notation.qmd) and Chapters 11 and 14. For a treatment
$k$ and covariate value $x$, $\mu_k(x)=\mathbb E[Y(k)\mid X=x]$ is the conditional mean potential outcome;
$g$ is the link of @def-link-function; the conditional contrast of $b$ versus $a$ on scale $g$ is
$\tau^g_{ab}(x)=g(\mu_b(x))-g(\mu_a(x))$ as in @def-effect-modifier; and a population $\mathcal P$ has
covariate density $f_{\mathcal P}$ with mean $\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P}=\int x\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx$.
This chapter owns result E.3 of the proof catalogue and introduces the ecological-bias material that
prepares Part IV.

### A running clinical example {#sec-limits-running}

Before any definitions, here is a concrete scenario we will return to at every transition. Read the whole
chapter with this picture in mind; the notation below is just a precise language for describing it.

::: {#exm-limits-psoriasis}
## Two biologics for plaque psoriasis
Consider moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Two biologic drugs, $A$ and $B$, have each been compared in
a randomized trial against the same standard systemic therapy $C$, but the two drugs have never been
compared head to head. We want the $A$-versus-$B$ contrast, and because both trials share the comparator
$C$ we can form it *indirectly* (an **anchored** comparison: both routes pass through the shared
comparator $C$).

The outcome is an unfavorable binary event, **treatment failure** (failing to reach an adequate skin
response by week 16); a larger risk is worse. One baseline covariate matters: prior biologic therapy,
$X=1$ for biologic-experienced patients and $X=0$ for biologic-naive patients. Prior therapy makes the
disease harder to control, so it raises the failure risk under the comparator $C$ and under biologic $B$
by the same amount, leaving the $B$-versus-$C$ benefit unchanged; but biologic $A$ acts through a pathway
unaffected by prior exposure, so its failure risk stays flat and its advantage over $C$ is *larger* in
experienced patients. Prior exposure is therefore an **effect modifier** of $A$ versus $C$ but not of $B$
versus $C$. The stratum-specific failure risks are

| stratum $x$ | $\mu_A(x)$ | $\mu_B(x)$ | $\mu_C(x)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $x=0$ (naive) | $0.30$ | $0.25$ | $0.40$ |
| $x=1$ (experienced) | $0.30$ | $0.45$ | $0.60$ |

The two trials enrolled different case mixes. The $A$-versus-$C$ trial recruited mostly biologic-naive
patients (prevalence of prior exposure $p_{AC}=0.2$); the $B$-versus-$C$ trial recruited mostly
experienced patients ($p_{BC}=0.8$). The decision (target) population for the $A$-versus-$B$
recommendation is evenly mixed, $p_{*}=0.5$.

**Why the shared comparator does not rescue us.** Sharing $C$ is what makes an indirect comparison
*possible*; it does not make the two trials exchangeable. The $A$-versus-$C$ trial measured $A$'s benefit
almost entirely in easy-to-treat patients, where that benefit is small, while the $B$-versus-$C$ trial
measured $B$'s benefit almost entirely in hard-to-treat patients. Subtracting the two trial-level effects
silently pits $A$'s benefit at one case mix against $B$'s benefit at another. That mismatch is exactly the
bias this chapter quantifies; @exm-limits-bucher-rd computes it and finds it large enough to reverse the
sign of the answer.

**Why it matters for a decision.** If the indirect estimate has the wrong sign, a health technology
assessment (for example a NICE appraisal, @phillippo2016tsd18) can recommend the inferior drug: patients
may be denied the better biologic, or a payer may fund one that is in truth no better. The bias below is
not academic; it can flip a reimbursement decision. This is why NICE Technical Support Document 18
(@phillippo2016tsd18) requires an indirect comparison to justify its constancy assumption before the
estimate is trusted. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Terms carried from earlier chapters.** A novice can treat the following as a glossary and refer back as
needed.

- **Contrast**: a difference of two treatments on a chosen scale, for example a risk difference or a log
  odds ratio. Throughout, "$a$ versus $b$", and the symbols $d_{ab}$ and $\tau_{ab}$, mean $b$ *relative
  to* $a$: $\tau^g_{ab}(x)=g(\mu_b(x))-g(\mu_a(x))$.
- **Anchored comparison**: an indirect $A$-versus-$B$ comparison in which both drugs are joined through a
  shared comparator $C$ (Chapter 14). The alternative, an **unanchored** comparison of absolute arm
  outcomes, is Chapter 26.
- **Effect modifier versus prognostic variable**: an effect modifier changes the *size of a contrast*
  across its levels; a purely prognostic variable shifts *both arms equally* and leaves the contrast
  unchanged (Chapter 11). This distinction is the most reused idea in the chapter.
- **Transitivity and consistency**: transitivity is the assumption that relative effects are comparable
  across trials so indirect and direct evidence agree; **consistency** is the same idea checked inside a
  network (Chapter 15). **Node-splitting** is the diagnostic that compares direct and indirect evidence at
  one contrast. **Heterogeneity** is unexplained trial-to-trial variation beyond sampling error (Chapter
  13); it is a variance phenomenon, distinct from the systematic bias studied here.
- **Link and inverse link $g,g^{-1}$**: $g$ maps a probability or mean to the linear-predictor scale;
  $g^{-1}$ maps back. For the logit link $g^{-1}$ is the logistic function $e^{\eta}/(1+e^{\eta})$; for the
  probit link $g^{-1}$ is the standard normal distribution function $\Phi$ (Chapter 7).
- **Directly collapsible scale**: a scale on which the population-level (marginal) effect equals the
  covariate-average of the per-stratum (conditional) effects. The risk difference is directly collapsible;
  the odds ratio is not (Chapter 11). We keep the qualifier "directly" to match Chapter 11; for this
  chapter you may read it as "collapsible."
- **Affine in $x$**: "linear plus a constant," a function of the form $a+b^{\top}x$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Sign convention.** A positive $\tau^g_{ab}(x)$ means $b$ scores higher than $a$ on scale $g$ at
covariate value $x$. On the risk-difference scale a positive $A$-versus-$B$ contrast means $B$ carries the
higher event risk; since the event is unfavorable, positive means $B$ is *worse* than $A$. The bias terms
$b_{AC},b_{BC}$ that appear in @eq-limits-bias are *bias contributions*, not treatment contrasts: the
lowercase $b$ is a bias, never "treatment $B$." $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Conditional and marginal relative effects {#sec-limits-setup}

Two relative effects can be attached to a population, and the distinction between them is the hinge of the
whole chapter. The first is the one a trial reports from its arm summaries; the second is the one a
patient-level regression estimates. They agree on a collapsible scale and diverge on a non-collapsible
one, and even when they agree they respond differently to a change of covariate distribution.

::: {#def-conditional-marginal-contrast}
## Marginal and average-conditional relative effects
Let $\mathcal P$ be a population with covariate density $f_{\mathcal P}$, let $g$ be a strictly increasing
link, and let $a,b$ be two treatments with conditional means $\mu_a(\cdot),\mu_b(\cdot)$. The **marginal
relative effect** of $b$ versus $a$ in $\mathcal P$ on scale $g$ is the contrast of marginalized arm means,
$$
d_{ab(\mathcal P)} \;=\; g\!\left(\int \mu_b(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx\right)-g\!\left(\int \mu_a(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx\right),
$$ {#eq-limits-marg}
exactly the quantity of @eq-bucher-reldef. The **average-conditional relative effect** of $b$ versus $a$
in $\mathcal P$ on scale $g$ is the covariate average of the conditional contrast,
$$
\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)} \;=\; \int \tau^g_{ab}(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx
\;=\; \int \bigl[g(\mu_b(x))-g(\mu_a(x))\bigr]\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx .
$$ {#eq-limits-avgcond}
The first marginalizes inside the link, the second outside. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader translation.* The single distinguishing mark is the tilde, so fix the mnemonic: **no tilde is
marginal**, the number a trial reports; **the tilde is average-conditional**, the number a patient-level
regression gives. The difference is *where the averaging sits relative to $g$*.

| Quantity | Recipe | Where the averaging happens |
|---|---|---|
| Marginal $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ (@eq-limits-marg) | average each arm's outcome over patients, then apply $g$ and subtract | inside the link: the average is inside the argument of $g$ |
| Average-conditional $\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ (@eq-limits-avgcond) | apply $g$ within each stratum and subtract, then average the per-stratum contrasts | outside the link: the average is applied after $g$ |

In a two-arm trial you observe only arm totals, so you can form the marginal effect $d$ directly. With
individual patient data you can estimate the per-patient contrast $\tau^g_{ab}(\cdot)$ and then average it,
giving $\tilde d$. On a directly collapsible scale (for example the risk difference) the two recipes give
the same number; on the odds-ratio scale they do not, and the difference is the non-collapsibility gap we
revisit in @sec-limits-surcharge.

The marginal effect @eq-limits-marg is what a two-arm trial estimates from its observed arm means, since a
randomized trial identifies $\int\mu_a f$ and $\int\mu_b f$ and then applies $g$ to each
(@prp-trial-unbiased). The average-conditional effect @eq-limits-avgcond is what an individual patient
data regression estimates, since such a regression identifies the conditional contrast $\tau^g_{ab}(\cdot)$
as a function of $x$ and then averages it. The relationship between the two is exactly the
collapsibility theory of Chapters 7 and 11.

::: {#prp-limits-collapse-link}
## When the two relative effects coincide
With the notation of @def-conditional-marginal-contrast:

1. If the scale $g$ is the identity (the risk-difference or mean-difference scale), then
   $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}=\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ for every population $\mathcal P$ and every pair of
   conditional means.
2. More generally, if the effect measure based on $g$ is **directly collapsible** over $X$ in the sense of
   @def-collapsibility, then $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}=\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ for every $\mathcal P$.
3. If $g$ is non-collapsible (the logit or log-hazard scale, @def-non-collapsibility,
   @thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr), the two differ in general; their difference is the non-collapsibility
   gap, a Jensen gap (@thm-jensen) for the nonlinear link.
:::

::: {.proof}
For (1), with $g$ the identity, linearity of the integral gives
$$
d_{ab(\mathcal P)}=\int\mu_b f-\int\mu_a f=\int(\mu_b-\mu_a)f=\int\tau^{\mathrm{id}}_{ab}(x)f(x)\,dx=\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)} .
$$
Statement (2) unpacks the definition of direct collapsibility. Direct collapsibility on scale $g$ means
precisely that the population marginal effect equals the covariate-weighted average of the conditional
effects, for *every* distribution of $X$; @eq-emcoll-direct is that statement. Applied to the contrast of
$b$ versus $a$ it reads $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}=\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$, which is what we want. The identity
scale is the canonical directly collapsible case, @prp-emcoll-rd-direct. For (3), take $g=\operatorname{logit}$
and a non-degenerate baseline; @thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr exhibits stratum means with constant conditional
effect for which the marginal effect strictly differs, so $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}\neq\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$.
The discrepancy is the difference between $g$ applied to an average and the average of $g$ applied
pointwise, which is the Jensen gap of @thm-jensen for the convex or concave pieces of $g$. $\square$
:::

*Reader translation.* On the risk-difference scale (and any directly collapsible scale) you may treat
"what the trial reports" and "the average of per-patient contrasts" as the *same number*. On the
odds-ratio or hazard-ratio scale you may not, and pretending otherwise is a second, independent source of
error that we isolate in @sec-limits-surcharge. For the first half of the chapter we work on a directly
collapsible scale, where @prp-limits-collapse-link lets us use $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ and
$\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ interchangeably and the algebra is exact; the identity scale is the running
example. The non-collapsible case, where the two relative effects come apart, returns in
@sec-limits-ecological as a second and independent source of bias. The pointwise additivity (sometimes
called conditional additivity) that powers Bucher's subtraction holds for the conditional contrasts
pointwise.

::: {#lem-limits-conditional-additivity}
## Pointwise additivity of conditional contrasts
For treatments $A,B,C$ and every covariate value $x$,
$$
\tau^g_{AB}(x) \;=\; \tau^g_{AC}(x)-\tau^g_{BC}(x).
$$ {#eq-limits-cond-additivity}
Consequently, on a directly collapsible scale, $\tilde d_{AB(\mathcal P)}=\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P)}-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P)}$ in every population $\mathcal P$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By definition $\tau^g_{ab}(x)=g(\mu_b(x))-g(\mu_a(x))$, so at fixed $x$ the three contrasts are
differences of the three numbers $g(\mu_A(x)),g(\mu_B(x)),g(\mu_C(x))$, and
$$
\tau^g_{AC}(x)-\tau^g_{BC}(x)=\bigl[g(\mu_C(x))-g(\mu_A(x))\bigr]-\bigl[g(\mu_C(x))-g(\mu_B(x))\bigr]=g(\mu_B(x))-g(\mu_A(x))=\tau^g_{AB}(x),
$$
which is @eq-limits-cond-additivity; this is @lem-relative-effect-algebra applied at the value $x$ rather
than to the marginal positions. Integrating both sides against $f_{\mathcal P}$ and using linearity gives
$\tilde d_{AB(\mathcal P)}=\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P)}-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P)}$. $\square$
:::

*Why this matters.* This pointwise identity is the *entire license* for Bucher's subtraction: at each
covariate value the $A$-versus-$B$ contrast is exactly the $A$-versus-$C$ contrast minus the
$B$-versus-$C$ contrast. Bucher subtracts the two trials' effects in the hope that this identity survives
averaging. The failure theorem below is precisely the statement that it need not survive, because the
three populations average the same conditional contrasts over *different* covariate distributions.

### The two faces of constancy {#sec-limits-two-constancies}

The constancy hypothesis of Bucher's theorem can now be split into its two natural strengths. Both will
appear in the failure analysis, and keeping them apart is what lets the theorem isolate the role of the
covariate distribution.

The first is **constancy of marginal relative effects**, the original transitivity of @def-transitivity:
the marginal effect $d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}$ is the same in every population. This is what Bucher's theorem
requires, and it is what we will show fails. The second is **conditional constancy of relative effects on
scale $g$**: there is a single function $\tau^g_{ab}(\cdot)$ such that, in every population in play, the
conditional contrast at covariate value $x$ equals $\tau^g_{ab}(x)$. Conditional constancy says the
per-stratum effect transports; it is the assumption that an individual-level effect estimated in one trial
is the same biological quantity in another population with the same within-stratum structure. In the
trial-methodology literature this is the **shared effect modifier assumption (SEMA)** of @phillippo2016tsd18;
"conditional constancy" is its estimand-level statement, and the two say the same thing. It is developed in
full as the anchored-adjustment assumption in Chapter 17. The point of the failure analysis is that
conditional constancy can hold while marginal constancy fails, and the gap between them is governed
entirely by the covariate distributions.

The distinction is easiest to hold onto as a table.

| Assumption | What it says | Needed by Bucher? | Can fail while the other holds? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marginal constancy (transitivity, @def-transitivity) | the *trial-reported* effect $d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}$ is one number across populations | yes: this is the hypothesis of @thm-bucher-unbiased | yes: it fails whenever an effect modifier is imbalanced |
| Conditional constancy (SEMA, @phillippo2016tsd18) | the *per-stratum* contrast $\tau^g_{ab}(x)$ is one function across populations | no | yes: it can hold even when marginal constancy fails |

Clinically: the biology of a treatment effect within, say, each prior-exposure stratum may transport
perfectly (conditional constancy), yet the trial-level average still changes if one trial enrolled mostly
experienced patients and the other mostly naive ones (marginal constancy fails). The whole chapter lives
in that gap.

::: {#lem-limits-em-breaks-transitivity}
## An imbalanced effect modifier breaks marginal constancy
Assume conditional constancy of relative effects on scale $g$, so the conditional contrast
$\tau^g_{ab}(\cdot)$ is the same function in two populations $\mathcal P_1,\mathcal P_2$. On a directly
collapsible scale the marginal relative effects are then $d_{ab(\mathcal P_i)}=\int\tau^g_{ab}(x)\,f_i(x)\,dx$,
and

1. if $X$ is **not** an effect modifier of $b$ versus $a$ on scale $g$, that is $\tau^g_{ab}(\cdot)\equiv c$
   is constant, then $d_{ab(\mathcal P_1)}=d_{ab(\mathcal P_2)}=c$ regardless of the covariate
   distributions; marginal constancy holds automatically;
2. if $X$ is an effect modifier on scale $g$, then there exist covariate distributions $f_1\neq f_2$ with
   $d_{ab(\mathcal P_1)}\neq d_{ab(\mathcal P_2)}$; marginal constancy fails.
:::

::: {.proof}
Under conditional constancy and direct collapsibility, @prp-limits-collapse-link(2) gives
$d_{ab(\mathcal P_i)}=\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P_i)}=\int\tau^g_{ab}(x)f_i(x)\,dx$. For (1), if
$\tau^g_{ab}\equiv c$ then $\int c\,f_i(x)\,dx=c\int f_i=c$ for either density, since a density integrates
to one; the two marginal effects equal the common value $c$. For (2), effect modification means
(@def-effect-modifier) there are points $x_1,x_2$ in the support with $\tau^g_{ab}(x_1)\neq\tau^g_{ab}(x_2)$.
If the support is discrete, take the two-point masses $f_1=\delta_{x_1}$ and $f_2=\delta_{x_2}$ directly;
then $d_{ab(\mathcal P_1)}=\tau^g_{ab}(x_1)\neq\tau^g_{ab}(x_2)=d_{ab(\mathcal P_2)}$ exactly, with no limit
needed. If the covariate is continuous, take a sequence of admissible densities $f_1^{(n)}$ concentrating
on shrinking neighborhoods of $x_1$; since $\tau^g_{ab}$ is bounded on the common support and continuous at
$x_1$, dominated convergence gives $\int\tau^g_{ab}\,f_1^{(n)}\to\tau^g_{ab}(x_1)$, and likewise
$\int\tau^g_{ab}\,f_2^{(n)}\to\tau^g_{ab}(x_2)$. For $n$ large enough the two marginal effects lie within
any prescribed tolerance of the unequal numbers $\tau^g_{ab}(x_1)$ and $\tau^g_{ab}(x_2)$, hence are
themselves unequal, so the two marginal effects differ. $\square$
:::

*Reader translation.* Part (1) is the formal statement that purely prognostic covariates do not threaten
an anchored comparison: a covariate that fails to modify the contrast leaves the marginal effect unchanged
however its distribution shifts, because its effect on the two arms cancels inside $\tau^g_{ab}$. This is
the machine-checked cancellation of @thm-emcoll-em-pv-distinct. Part (2) is the mechanism of failure: only
effect modifiers, and only when their distribution differs across populations, can move the marginal
effect and so break the transitivity that Bucher's theorem assumes. In the running example
(@exm-limits-psoriasis), prior exposure modifies $A$ versus $C$, so the differing case mixes of the two
trials will move that trial's reported effect; it does not modify $B$ versus $C$, so the $B$-versus-$C$
trial's imbalance turns out to be harmless.

## The failure-of-Bucher theorem {#sec-limits-failure-bucher}

We now compute the bias exactly. The setup is the anchored triangle of Chapter 14 (three treatments joined
through the shared comparator $C$): an $AC$ trial in population $\mathcal P_{AC}$, a $BC$ trial in
population $\mathcal P_{BC}$, and a target population $\mathcal P^{*}$ in which we wish to report the
$A$-versus-$B$ contrast. Conditional constancy holds, so the conditional contrasts $\tau^g_{AC}(\cdot)$ and
$\tau^g_{BC}(\cdot)$ are common to all three populations; the covariate distributions $f_{AC},f_{BC},f_{*}$
may all differ. The target estimand is the average-conditional contrast in $\mathcal P^{*}$,
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*}) \;=\; \int \tau^g_{AB}(x)\,f_{*}(x)\,dx
\;=\; \int\bigl[\tau^g_{AC}(x)-\tau^g_{BC}(x)\bigr]f_{*}(x)\,dx ,
$$ {#eq-limits-target}
the second equality by @lem-limits-conditional-additivity. Each trial reports its own average-conditional
contrast, $\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\int\tau^g_{AC}f_{AC}$ and
$\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\int\tau^g_{BC}f_{BC}$, and the Bucher procedure subtracts them.

Four quantities are now in play, and it is worth pinning down which is which before the theorem. This is
the estimand roadmap for the rest of the chapter.

| Symbol | Plain meaning | Estimated from | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ (@eq-limits-marg) | marginal effect: apply $g$ to each arm's average outcome, then subtract | a two-arm trial's arm summaries | this is the number that shifts when an effect modifier is imbalanced |
| $\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ (@eq-limits-avgcond) | average-conditional effect: per-stratum contrast, averaged over the population | an individual-patient-data regression | on a collapsible scale it equals $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$; it is what Bucher implicitly subtracts |
| $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$ (@eq-limits-target) | the target $A$-versus-$B$ contrast in the decision population | the estimand we *want* | this is what a valid indirect comparison must deliver |
| $d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}}$ | the Bucher estimand $\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ | subtracting the two trials' contrasts | what standard NMA delivers; differs from the target by @eq-limits-bias |

Before the general integral statement, here is the binary-covariate special case. It contains the whole
idea in one line of arithmetic, and the general theorem is its integral generalization.

::: {#prp-limits-binary-bias}
## The binary-covariate bias
In the anchored triangle above, suppose $X\in\{0,1\}$ is binary with $\Pr(X=1)$ equal to
$p_{AC},p_{BC},p_{*}$ in the three populations, and conditional constancy holds. Write the
**effect-modification jump** of the $t$-versus-$C$ contrast as
$s_{tC}=\tau^g_{tC}(1)-\tau^g_{tC}(0)$, for $t\in\{A,B\}$. Then the asymptotic bias of the unadjusted
indirect comparison $d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}}=\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$
relative to the target @eq-limits-target is
$$
d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}}-\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})
\;=\; s_{AC}\,(p_{AC}-p_{*}) \;-\; s_{BC}\,(p_{BC}-p_{*}) .
$$ {#eq-limits-binary-bias}
:::

::: {.proof}
For a binary covariate, $\tilde d_{tC(\mathcal P_j)}=(1-p_j)\tau^g_{tC}(0)+p_j\tau^g_{tC}(1)$ in any
population with prevalence $p_j$. Applying this to the trial population $p_{tC}$ and to the target $p_{*}$
and differencing,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde d_{tC(\mathcal P_{tC})}-\int\tau^g_{tC}f_{*}
&=\bigl[(1-p_{tC})\tau^g_{tC}(0)+p_{tC}\tau^g_{tC}(1)\bigr]-\bigl[(1-p_{*})\tau^g_{tC}(0)+p_{*}\tau^g_{tC}(1)\bigr]\\
&=\tau^g_{tC}(0)\,(p_{*}-p_{tC})+\tau^g_{tC}(1)\,(p_{tC}-p_{*})\\
&=\bigl[\tau^g_{tC}(1)-\tau^g_{tC}(0)\bigr](p_{tC}-p_{*})=s_{tC}\,(p_{tC}-p_{*}).
\end{aligned}
$$
Call this $b_{tC}$. Subtracting the $BC$ term from the $AC$ term and using additivity @eq-limits-cond-additivity
inside the target gives $d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}}-\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=b_{AC}-b_{BC}
=s_{AC}(p_{AC}-p_{*})-s_{BC}(p_{BC}-p_{*})$. $\square$
:::

*Reader translation.* On a binary effect modifier, each contrast's bias is its **effect-modification jump
times how much the trial over- or under-represents the high-risk stratum relative to the target**. No
modification ($s_{tC}=0$) or no imbalance ($p_{tC}=p_{*}$) kills that term. For the psoriasis network of
@exm-limits-psoriasis on the risk-difference scale, $s_{AC}=\tau_{AC}(1)-\tau_{AC}(0)=0.30-0.10=0.20$ and
$s_{BC}=0.15-0.15=0$, while $p_{AC}-p_{*}=0.2-0.5=-0.3$; the bias is
$0.20\cdot(-0.3)-0=-0.06$. The $A$-versus-$C$ trial under-represents the hard-to-treat stratum, and
$A$-versus-$C$ is the *modified* contrast, so the indirect comparison inherits a $-0.06$ bias.
@exm-limits-bucher-rd shows this is enough to flip the sign of the answer.

::: {#thm-failure-of-bucher}
## Failure of Bucher under differential effect modification
Fix a treatment triple $\{A,B,C\}$ and a scale $g$, and assume conditional constancy of relative effects on
scale $g$, with common conditional contrasts $\tau^g_{AC}(\cdot),\tau^g_{BC}(\cdot)$. Let the Bucher
estimand built from the two trials' average-conditional contrasts be
$$
d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}} \;=\; \tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}
\;=\; \int\tau^g_{AC}(x)\,f_{AC}(x)\,dx-\int\tau^g_{BC}(x)\,f_{BC}(x)\,dx ,
$$
and let the target be $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$ of @eq-limits-target. Then the
asymptotic bias of the unadjusted indirect comparison is
$$
d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}}-\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})
\;=\; \underbrace{\int\tau^g_{AC}(x)\,[f_{AC}(x)-f_{*}(x)]\,dx}_{\textstyle b_{AC}}
\;-\; \underbrace{\int\tau^g_{BC}(x)\,[f_{BC}(x)-f_{*}(x)]\,dx}_{\textstyle b_{BC}} .
$$ {#eq-limits-bias}
Moreover:

1. (Vanishing under no modification.) For each contrast $t\in\{A,B\}$, the term $b_{tC}$ vanishes for
   **every** pair of covariate distributions $(f_{tC},f_{*})$ if and only if $\tau^g_{tC}$ is constant on
   the common support, that is, if and only if $X$ is not an effect modifier of $t$ versus $C$ on scale
   $g$. In particular, if neither contrast is modified, the bias is zero for all covariate distributions.

2. (Genuineness of the bias.) If $X$ is an effect modifier of at least one of $A$ versus $C$ or $B$ versus
   $C$ on scale $g$, then there exist covariate distributions making the bias @eq-limits-bias nonzero.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @thm-bucher-unbiased, the Bucher subtraction would equal the target contrast if each trial reported the
population-free network effect, that is if marginal constancy held; the present hypotheses grant only
conditional constancy, and we compute the residual directly. Linearity of the integral gives, for the $AC$
contrast,
$$
\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\int\tau^g_{AC}(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx
=\int\tau^g_{AC}(x)f_{AC}(x)\,dx-\int\tau^g_{AC}(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx
=\int\tau^g_{AC}(x)\,[f_{AC}(x)-f_{*}(x)]\,dx=b_{AC},
$$
and identically $\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\int\tau^g_{BC}f_{*}=b_{BC}$. Subtracting the second display
from the first and using the additivity @eq-limits-cond-additivity inside the target,
$$
d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}}-\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})
=\Bigl(\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\textstyle\int\tau^g_{AC}f_{*}\Bigr)-\Bigl(\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\int\tau^g_{BC}f_{*}\Bigr)=b_{AC}-b_{BC},
$$
which is @eq-limits-bias.

For (1), suppose first that $\tau^g_{tC}\equiv c$ is constant. Then
$b_{tC}=c\int[f_{tC}(x)-f_{*}(x)]\,dx=c\,(1-1)=0$, since each density integrates to one; this holds for any
pair of distributions. Conversely suppose $\tau^g_{tC}$ is not constant, so there are support points
$x_1,x_2$ with $\tau^g_{tC}(x_1)\neq\tau^g_{tC}(x_2)$. Choosing $f_{tC}$ concentrated near $x_2$ and $f_{*}$
near $x_1$ (point masses if the support is discrete) gives
$b_{tC}\to\tau^g_{tC}(x_2)-\tau^g_{tC}(x_1)\neq 0$, so the term does not vanish for all pairs. Hence
$b_{tC}\equiv 0$ over all distribution pairs if and only if $\tau^g_{tC}$ is constant, i.e. $X$ is not an
effect modifier for $t$ versus $C$. The final clause of (1) is the case where both contrasts are constant,
so $b_{AC}=b_{BC}=0$ identically.

For (2), if (say) $X$ modifies the $A$-versus-$C$ contrast, the converse direction of (1) furnishes a pair
$(f_{AC},f_{*})$ with $b_{AC}\neq0$; choosing $f_{BC}=f_{*}$ makes $b_{BC}=0$, so the total bias is
$b_{AC}\neq0$. The same construction works if $X$ modifies the $B$-versus-$C$ contrast. $\square$
:::

This is result E.3 of the proof catalogue, and @prp-limits-binary-bias is its two-point special case
($b_{tC}=s_{tC}(p_{tC}-p_{*})$ when $X$ is binary). The bias decomposition @eq-limits-bias has a
transparent reading. Each term $b_{tC}$ is the difference between the trial-population mean of the
conditional contrast and its target-population mean; it is a covariance-like quantity, the inner product of
the effect-modification function $\tau^g_{tC}$ with the signed measure $f_{tC}-f_{*}$. Physically, a
positive $b_{AC}$ says trial $AC$ *over-represents the strata where $A$'s advantage is large* relative to
the target: it sampled too many high-contrast patients, so its reported $A$-versus-$C$ effect overshoots
the target average. The bias is large when the contrast varies steeply over $x$ (strong effect
modification) and when the trial and target distributions are far apart (strong imbalance), and it is
exactly zero when either factor is absent. The cure is now legible in the formula: replace $f_{tC}$ by
$f_{*}$, that is, reweight or re-regress each trial's conditional contrast to the target covariate
distribution, and each $b_{tC}$ collapses to zero. That operation is population adjustment.

*Why this matters.* Standard NMA computes $d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}}$; the estimand a decision needs is
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$. The theorem says these differ by a term that a health
researcher can neither see in the standard error nor remove without extra data, which is the entire reason
population-adjusted methods exist.

We put numbers on the theorem immediately, in the running example.

::: {#exm-limits-bucher-rd}
## A sign-reversing Bucher bias on the risk-difference scale
This is the psoriasis network of @exm-limits-psoriasis with the arithmetic filled in. The outcome is a
binary event (treatment failure, an unfavorable outcome, so larger risk is worse), $X\in\{0,1\}$ is prior
biologic exposure, and we work on the identity (risk-difference) scale, $g=\mathrm{id}$, which is directly
collapsible (@prp-emcoll-rd-direct). Conditional constancy holds, so the stratum risks below are common to
all three populations:

| stratum $x$ | $\mu_A(x)$ | $\mu_B(x)$ | $\mu_C(x)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $x=0$ | $0.30$ | $0.25$ | $0.40$ |
| $x=1$ | $0.30$ | $0.45$ | $0.60$ |

so treatment $A$ has constant risk $0.30$ while $B$ and $C$ have stratum-dependent risk. The conditional
contrasts on the risk-difference scale, $\tau_{tC}(x)=\mu_C(x)-\mu_t(x)$, are
$$
\tau_{AC}(0)=0.40-0.30=0.10,\quad \tau_{AC}(1)=0.60-0.30=0.30,
$$
$$
\tau_{BC}(0)=0.40-0.25=0.15,\quad \tau_{BC}(1)=0.60-0.45=0.15 .
$$
Thus $X$ **is** an effect modifier of $A$ versus $C$ (the contrast moves from $0.10$ to $0.30$) and is
**not** an effect modifier of $B$ versus $C$ (the contrast is $0.15$ in both strata). The target contrast
$\tau_{AB}(x)=\mu_B(x)-\mu_A(x)$ is $\tau_{AB}(0)=0.25-0.30=-0.05$ and $\tau_{AB}(1)=0.45-0.30=0.15$, which
matches $\tau_{AC}-\tau_{BC}$ stratum by stratum as @lem-limits-conditional-additivity requires.

The three populations differ only in the prevalence $p=\Pr(X=1)$ of the effect modifier:
$$
p_{AC}=0.2,\qquad p_{BC}=0.8,\qquad p_{*}=0.5 .
$$

**Trial reports.** Each trial reports its average-conditional contrast, which on this scale equals what its
arm means give:
$$
\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=(1-p_{AC})\,\tau_{AC}(0)+p_{AC}\,\tau_{AC}(1)=0.8(0.10)+0.2(0.30)=0.14,
$$
$$
\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(1-p_{BC})\,\tau_{BC}(0)+p_{BC}\,\tau_{BC}(1)=0.15 .
$$

**Bucher estimand.**
$$
d_{AB}^{\mathrm{Bucher}}=\tilde d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=0.14-0.15=-0.01 .
$$

**Target.**
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},\mathrm{id}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=(1-p_{*})\,\tau_{AB}(0)+p_{*}\,\tau_{AB}(1)=0.5(-0.05)+0.5(0.15)=0.05 .
$$

**Bias.** The unadjusted indirect comparison reports $-0.01$ when the true target risk difference is
$+0.05$: it is biased by $-0.06$, and it has the **wrong sign**. On the unadjusted estimate $B$ looks
marginally protective relative to $A$; in truth $B$ raises the event risk by five percentage points in the
target population. In clinical terms, the indirect comparison would recommend $B$ when $A$ is in fact the
better drug.

**Verification through @eq-limits-bias.** The bias decomposition gives
$$
b_{AC}=\tau_{AC}(0)\,[(1-p_{AC})-(1-p_{*})]+\tau_{AC}(1)\,[p_{AC}-p_{*}]=0.10(0.3)+0.30(-0.3)=0.03-0.09=-0.06,
$$
$$
b_{BC}=0.15\cdot\bigl([(1-p_{BC})-(1-p_{*})]+[p_{BC}-p_{*}]\bigr)=0.15\cdot 0=0,
$$
the second vanishing because $\tau_{BC}$ is constant, exactly @thm-failure-of-bucher(1). The total
$b_{AC}-b_{BC}=-0.06-0=-0.06$ reproduces the bias, and matches the binary formula
$s_{AC}(p_{AC}-p_{*})=0.20\cdot(-0.3)$ of @prp-limits-binary-bias. Note that $B$ versus $C$ is the more
imbalanced contrast, $p_{BC}=0.8$ against $p_{*}=0.5$, yet it contributes nothing, because $X$ does not
modify it; all the bias comes from $A$ versus $C$, which is only modestly imbalanced but is modified.

**The cure.** Reweighting the modified contrast to the target distribution replaces $p_{AC}$ by $p_{*}$:
$\int\tau_{AC}f_{*}=0.5(0.10)+0.5(0.30)=0.20$, and then $0.20-0.15=0.05$ recovers the target exactly. That
reweighting is what a population-adjusted method performs. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The corollary that follows is the single most useful practical fact in the chapter for an analyst: it says
which covariates you actually have to worry about.

Before the algebra, the plain reason. In a *contrast* on a collapsible scale, any covariate effect that
enters both arms by the same amount cancels: if a covariate raises the failure risk under $A$ and under $C$
equally, it leaves $\mu_C-\mu_A$ untouched, so it cannot bias the $A$-versus-$C$ contrast no matter how
imbalanced it is. Only a covariate that changes the *difference* between the arms survives. That is the
whole content of the corollary. The following one-line table is worth memorizing.

| Covariate role | Effect on the two arms | Effect on the contrast $\tau^g$ | Anchored ITC consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purely prognostic (e.g., a severity marker that raises failure risk under both $A$ and $C$ equally) | shifts both arms by the same amount | unchanged: it cancels | imbalance is harmless; contributes no Bucher bias |
| Effect modifier (e.g., prior biologic exposure) | shifts the arms by different amounts | changes with the covariate | imbalance biases the indirect comparison |

::: {#cor-limits-pv-no-bias}
## Purely prognostic covariates contribute no Bucher bias
A covariate that is a prognostic variable (@def-prognostic-variable) for the arms but is not an effect
modifier of $A$ versus $C$ or of $B$ versus $C$ on scale $g$ contributes zero to the bias @eq-limits-bias,
however imbalanced its distribution across $\mathcal P_{AC},\mathcal P_{BC},\mathcal P^{*}$.

[machine-checked: `theories/EffectModifiers.v`, `Theorem anchored_PV_cancellation`]
:::

::: {.proof}
Decompose the covariate vector as $X=(X_{\mathrm{EM}},W)$, where $W$ is the purely prognostic component.
By the definition of "not an effect modifier," the conditional contrast does not depend on $W$:
$\tau^g_{tC}(x_{\mathrm{EM}},w)=\tau^g_{tC}(x_{\mathrm{EM}})$ for all $w$, for $t\in\{A,B\}$. This is the
content of `anchored_PV_cancellation` in the Coq development: if the contrast $\mu_t(\cdot,w)-\mu_C(\cdot,w)$
on the model scale is constant in $w$, it equals its value at any other $w'$. Now write $f_{tC}$ and
$f_{*}$ as joint densities of $(X_{\mathrm{EM}},W)$. Because $\tau^g_{tC}$ does not depend on $w$, we may
interchange the order of integration and integrate out $W$ first; this interchange is Fubini's theorem,
valid because $\tau^g_{tC}$ is bounded on the support and the densities are integrable. Integrating each
density's $W$-slice down to its $X_{\mathrm{EM}}$-marginal $f^{\mathrm{EM}}(x_{\mathrm{EM}})=\int f(x_{\mathrm{EM}},w)\,dw$,
$$
b_{tC}=\int\tau^g_{tC}(x_{\mathrm{EM}})\Bigl[\int\bigl(f_{tC}(x_{\mathrm{EM}},w)-f_{*}(x_{\mathrm{EM}},w)\bigr)\,dw\Bigr]dx_{\mathrm{EM}}
=\int\tau^g_{tC}(x_{\mathrm{EM}})\,[f^{\mathrm{EM}}_{tC}(x_{\mathrm{EM}})-f^{\mathrm{EM}}_{*}(x_{\mathrm{EM}})]\,dx_{\mathrm{EM}},
$$
which depends only on the marginal distribution of the effect-modifying component $X_{\mathrm{EM}}$. Any
imbalance confined to $W$ has integrated away and contributes nothing. $\square$
:::

@cor-limits-pv-no-bias is the rigorous form of the slogan that "prognostic variables cancel in anchored
comparisons." It is the precise reason an anchored adjustment need balance only the effect modifiers, a
fact that Chapter 17 turns into the central anchored-consistency theorem and that makes anchored methods
far less data-hungry than unanchored ones. The cancellation is purely a property of the contrast; it has
no analogue when one compares absolute arm outcomes, which is why unanchored comparison (Chapter 26) must
control prognostic variables too.

::: {.remark}
**Warning: the standard error cannot see this bias.** The bias @eq-limits-bias is a deterministic
functional of the true conditional contrasts and covariate distributions. It does not depend on the trial
sample sizes and does not vanish as they grow; it is a bias, not a variance. The Bucher standard error of
@thm-bucher-variance estimates only the sampling variability of $\hat d_{AC}$ and $\hat d_{BC}$ around
their own population means, so it is blind to @eq-limits-bias entirely. A confidently narrow indirect
confidence interval can be centered on the wrong number. This is the formal sense in which a transitivity
failure is undetectable from the precision of the estimate alone: a tight interval buys you no protection
here. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Warning: in the anchored triangle this bias is untestable.** When the same contrast carries both direct
and indirect evidence, the two can be compared, and a discrepancy signals that some constancy assumption
has failed; this is the node-splitting and consistency machinery of Chapter 15 (@def-node-splitting,
@thm-consistency-closure). But in the minimal anchored triangle there is no direct $A$-versus-$B$ evidence,
nothing to compare the indirect estimate against, and @eq-limits-bias is then untestable from the trial
outcomes. It can be assessed only by examining the covariate distributions $f_{AC},f_{BC},f_{*}$ and asking
whether any effect modifier is imbalanced, which requires knowing which covariates modify the effect and on
what scale. That is a substantive, external judgment, and the reason NICE Technical Support Document 18
(@phillippo2016tsd18) insists that an indirect comparison justify constancy before relying on it.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### The non-collapsibility surcharge {#sec-limits-surcharge}

So far we worked on a directly collapsible scale, where the trial-reported marginal contrast and the
average-conditional contrast are one number. On a non-collapsible scale a *second* discrepancy appears,
independent of any imbalance, and it is worth isolating because health researchers meet it constantly:
everyone knows odds ratios "behave strangely."

::: {.remark}
**The non-collapsibility surcharge.** @thm-failure-of-bucher is exact for the average-conditional estimand
@eq-limits-target on any scale, and on a directly collapsible scale (identity, log risk ratio) it is also
the exact bias of the marginal contrast a trial reports, by @prp-limits-collapse-link. On a non-collapsible
scale, such as the log odds ratio, the trial's reported marginal contrast $d_{tC(\mathcal P_j)}$ is not the
average-conditional $\tilde d_{tC(\mathcal P_j)}$, and a second discrepancy, the non-collapsibility gap, is
added to @eq-limits-bias. That second gap is itself a Jensen gap for the nonlinear link. We illustrate it
numerically just below, and the same mechanism reappears as ecological bias in @sec-limits-ecological. The
two effects compound: an imbalanced effect modifier biases the indirect comparison, and a nonlinear link
distorts what each trial reports in the first place. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**A numeric illustration in its purest form.** Take a single trial, a treatment versus a control, and a
binary covariate $X$ balanced at $\Pr(X=1)=0.5$, so there is no imbalance at all. Let the control risks be
$\mu_0(0)=0.1$ and $\mu_0(1)=0.5$, and let the conditional odds ratio be a *constant* $3$ in both strata,
so $X$ is not even an effect modifier. Solving for the treated risks gives $\mu_1(0)=0.25$ and
$\mu_1(1)=0.75$, and the conditional log odds ratio is $\log 3=1.0986$ in each stratum. The marginalized
arm risks are $\bar\mu_0=(0.1+0.5)/2=0.30$ and $\bar\mu_1=(0.25+0.75)/2=0.50$, so the marginal odds ratio is
$$
\frac{0.50/0.50}{0.30/0.70}=\frac{1}{3/7}=\frac{7}{3}\approx 2.33,\qquad \log\frac{7}{3}=0.8473 .
$$
Even with the conditional odds ratio identical in both strata and the covariate perfectly balanced, the
marginal odds ratio is $2.33$, not $3$: the marginal log odds ratio $0.847$ sits *below* the conditional
$1.099$. That gap, about $0.25$, is pure non-collapsibility; it owes nothing to imbalance and would be
present in a single perfectly balanced trial.

The two problems are genuinely separate, and it helps to tabulate them.

| Source of discrepancy | What it is | When it appears | Scale dependence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Effect-modifier imbalance (Bucher bias) | @eq-limits-bias: trial and target case mixes differ on a modified contrast | whenever an effect modifier is imbalanced across trial and target | present on every scale, including collapsible ones |
| Non-collapsibility surcharge | the marginal (trial-reported) contrast differs from the average-conditional contrast | whenever the link is nonlinear (odds ratio, hazard ratio), even with balanced covariates | only on non-collapsible scales |

In a real anchored odds-ratio comparison the two effects add: each trial's reported marginal log odds
ratio already differs from its average-conditional log odds ratio by a non-collapsibility gap (this
illustration), and then the imbalance of effect modifiers biases the subtraction (@eq-limits-bias).
@exr-limits-logit-compound asks you to compute both for the psoriasis network of @exm-limits-bucher-rd and
confirm that the total discrepancy exceeds the $-0.06$ of the risk-difference analysis.

## Aggregate meta-regression and ecological bias {#sec-limits-ecological}

@thm-failure-of-bucher shows that the cure is to reweight each conditional contrast to the target
covariate distribution. The obstacle, in the typical health-technology-assessment setting, is that the
analyst has individual patient data (IPD) for at most one trial and only **aggregate data** (AgD), the
covariate means $\bar{\mathbf x}_j$ and arm-level outcome summaries, for the others. A natural idea is to
sidestep the need for IPD by regressing trial-level treatment effects on trial-level covariate means, an
**aggregate-level meta-regression**, and to use the fitted slope to adjust for imbalance. This section
proves that the idea fails: the aggregate slope is not the individual-level effect-modifier coefficient,
and the error has a definite source and sign. The phenomenon is the **ecological fallacy**, and the error
is **ecological bias**.

**The analyst's temptation, and the two slopes it confuses.** Put yourself in the analyst's chair: "I do
not have patient-level data for the other trial, but I do have its mean covariate, say mean prior-exposure
prevalence or mean age. If I collect several trials, each reporting a covariate mean $\bar x_j$ and a
treatment effect $D_j$, surely the slope of $D_j$ against $\bar x_j$ tells me how the effect changes with
the covariate?" Concretely, suppose three trials report

| trial | covariate mean $\bar x_j$ | trial contrast $D_j$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $0.0$ | $0.332$ |
| 2 | $0.5$ | $0.427$ |
| 3 | $1.0$ | $0.521$ |

The fitted between-trial slope is $(0.521-0.332)/1.0\approx 0.19$. Call it $b_2$. The temptation is to read
$b_2$ as the effect-modification coefficient. But there are two different objects here:

- $b_2$ is the **between-trial slope**: how a *trial's* aggregate contrast changes as the *trial's mean*
  covariate changes, read off aggregate summaries.
- $\beta_2$ is the **within-patient interaction**: how *one patient's* contrast changes as *that patient's*
  own covariate changes, a coefficient in the individual-level model.

@thm-ecological-norecovery proves that these are not equal; $b_2$ is a strictly *shrunken* image of
$\beta_2$. In the numbers above the true $\beta_2$ is $0.6$, not $0.19$. The root cause is one line of
calculus: the aggregate arm mean is an average of a nonlinear inverse link over the covariate
distribution, and that is not the inverse link evaluated at the average covariate.

::: {#lem-limits-aggregation-jensen}
## The aggregation gap is a Jensen gap
Let the individual-level model have link $g$ and a linear predictor $\eta_t(x)$ that is affine in $x$ (that
is, of the form $a+b^{\top}x$, linear plus a constant), so the conditional mean of arm $t$ is
$\mu_t(x)=g^{-1}(\eta_t(x))$. For a population with covariate density $f$ and mean
$\bar x=\int x\,f(x)\,dx$,
$$
\int g^{-1}(\eta_t(x))\,f(x)\,dx \;\neq\; g^{-1}\!\Bigl(\int\eta_t(x)\,f(x)\,dx\Bigr)=g^{-1}(\eta_t(\bar x))
\qquad\text{in general.}
$$ {#eq-limits-jensen-gap}
If $g^{-1}$ is convex the left side is the larger; if $g^{-1}$ is concave the right side is the larger; if
$g^{-1}$ is affine on the range of $\eta_t$, the two are equal for every $f$. When $g^{-1}$ is strictly
convex or strictly concave on that range and $X$ is non-degenerate, the inequality is strict.
:::

::: {.proof}
Because $\eta_t$ is affine, $\int\eta_t(x)f(x)\,dx=\eta_t(\bar x)$ exactly, which gives the displayed
equality on the right. Apply Jensen's inequality (@thm-jensen) to the random variable $\eta_t(X)$ with the
convex function $\varphi=g^{-1}$: $\varphi(\mathbb E[\eta_t(X)])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(\eta_t(X))]$, that is
$g^{-1}(\eta_t(\bar x))\le\int g^{-1}(\eta_t(x))f(x)\,dx$, with strict inequality when $g^{-1}$ is strictly
convex and $\eta_t(X)$ is non-degenerate, the latter holding when $X$ is non-degenerate and the affine map
$\eta_t$ is non-constant. The concave case is the same inequality reversed, applied to $-g^{-1}$. If
$g^{-1}$ is affine on the range of $\eta_t$ then it commutes with the expectation and the two sides agree
for every $f$. $\square$
:::

*Reader translation.* The load-bearing move is that Jensen is applied to the random variable $\eta_t(X)$,
the *linear predictor*, not to $X$ itself; the convex function is the inverse link $g^{-1}$. In plain
words: with a curved inverse link, **the average of the patients' risks is not the risk of the average
patient**. Evaluating the model at the mean covariate (the "plug-in") therefore misses the true aggregate
mean whenever the link is nonlinear.

**A one-line numeric check.** Take the probit inverse link $g^{-1}=\Phi$ and $\eta(X)=0.5+X$ with
$X\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$. The true aggregate mean, using the Gaussian identity @eq-limits-probit-integral
below, is $\mathbb E[\Phi(0.5+X)]=\Phi(0.5/\sqrt{2})=\Phi(0.354)\approx 0.638$, whereas the plug-in value is
$\Phi(0.5)\approx 0.691$. The plug-in overstates the aggregate risk by about five percentage points; that
gap is the Jensen gap, and it is exactly the quantity we now name.

The only link for which @eq-limits-jensen-gap is an equality for all covariate distributions is the one
whose inverse is affine, namely the identity link, where $g^{-1}$ is the identity map. For every nonlinear
link, the logit with $g^{-1}(\eta)=e^{\eta}/(1+e^{\eta})$, the log with $g^{-1}(\eta)=e^{\eta}$, the probit
with $g^{-1}=\Phi$, the aggregation gap is generically nonzero. We name it.

::: {#def-ecological-bias}
## Ecological (aggregation) bias
Let an individual-level outcome model have link $g$ and a linear predictor $\eta_t(x)$ affine in the
covariates $x$, so that the conditional mean of arm $t$ is $\mu_t(x)=g^{-1}(\eta_t(x))$. For a population
with covariate density $f$ and mean $\bar x=\int x\,f(x)\,dx$, the **aggregate (population-averaged) arm
mean** is
$$
\bar\mu_t \;=\; \int g^{-1}(\eta_t(x))\,f(x)\,dx ,
$$
and the **plug-in arm mean** is $g^{-1}(\eta_t(\bar x))$, obtained by evaluating the individual model at the
mean covariate. The **ecological bias** (or aggregation bias) of arm $t$ in this population is the
discrepancy between them,
$$
\mathrm{EB}_t(f) \;=\; g^{-1}(\eta_t(\bar x))-\int g^{-1}(\eta_t(x))\,f(x)\,dx \;=\; g^{-1}(\eta_t(\bar x))-\bar\mu_t .
$$ {#eq-ecological-bias}
At the level of the relative effect, suppose the individual interaction slope of the contrast
$\eta_1(x)-\eta_0(x)$ in $x$ is $\beta_2$ (the effect-modification coefficient of @lem-emcoll-interaction),
and let $b_2$ be the slope in $\bar x$ of the aggregate marginal contrast $g(\bar\mu_1)-g(\bar\mu_0)$
regarded as a function of the covariate mean across populations. The **ecological bias of the
effect-modification coefficient** is
$$
\mathrm{EB}_{\mathrm{coef}} \;=\; b_2-\beta_2 ,
$$ {#eq-limits-coef-eb}
the difference between the between-trial (ecological) slope $b_2$ and the within-patient interaction
$\beta_2$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

By @lem-limits-aggregation-jensen the arm-level ecological bias @eq-ecological-bias is nonzero whenever the
link is nonlinear and the covariate is non-degenerate, with sign fixed by the convexity of $g^{-1}$. The
ecological bias of the coefficient @eq-limits-coef-eb is the consequential one for indirect comparison,
because it is the slope $\beta_2$, the strength of effect modification, that the adjustment in
@thm-failure-of-bucher needs. We now compute $b_2$ in closed form for the probit link and a normal
covariate, the one case where the aggregation integral @eq-ecological-bias is elementary, and read off the
bias exactly.

First the computational tool. The next lemma is a self-contained calculation; we flag it as such and use
it only inside the theorem that follows.

::: {#lem-limits-probit-integral}
## The Gaussian probit integral
Let $Z\sim\mathcal N(m,\sigma^2)$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then
$$
\mathbb E[\Phi(a+bZ)] \;=\; \Phi\!\left(\frac{a+bm}{\sqrt{1+b^2\sigma^2}}\right).
$$ {#eq-limits-probit-integral}
:::

::: {.proof}
Recall the meaning of $\Phi$: for a standard normal $U\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, the value $\Phi(t)=P(U\le t)$
is *literally* the probability that $U$ falls at or below $t$. Let $U\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ be independent of
$Z$. Then for fixed $Z$ this reading gives $\Phi(a+bZ)=P(U\le a+bZ\mid Z)$. Taking expectations over $Z$
and using the law of total probability,
$$
\mathbb E[\Phi(a+bZ)]=P(U\le a+bZ)=P(U-bZ\le a).
$$
The variable $U-bZ$ is a linear combination of independent normals. Its moment generating function is, by
@thm-mgf-sum applied to $U$ and $-bZ$,
$$
M_{U-bZ}(s)=M_U(s)\,M_{-bZ}(s)=e^{\frac12 s^2}\cdot e^{-bms+\frac12 b^2\sigma^2 s^2}=\exp\!\Bigl(-bm\,s+\tfrac12(1+b^2\sigma^2)s^2\Bigr),
$$
which is the moment generating function of $\mathcal N(-bm,\,1+b^2\sigma^2)$; by uniqueness
(@thm-mgf-uniqueness) that is the law of $U-bZ$. Standardizing,
$$
P(U-bZ\le a)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{a-(-bm)}{\sqrt{1+b^2\sigma^2}}\right)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{a+bm}{\sqrt{1+b^2\sigma^2}}\right),
$$
which is @eq-limits-probit-integral. $\square$
:::

We can now state the attenuation theorem. Because several symbols enter at once, here is the map to keep
beside the statement.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $a_0,a_1$ | arm intercepts (control, treated) on the probit scale |
| $\rho_0,\rho_1$ | arm slopes in the covariate $x$ on the probit scale |
| $\beta_2=\rho_1-\rho_0$ | within-patient effect-modification coefficient (the target quantity) |
| $b_2$ | between-trial (ecological) slope from aggregate meta-regression |
| $\sigma^2$ | common within-trial covariate variance |
| $\bar x_j$ | covariate mean of trial $j$ |
| $\Phi,\Phi^{-1}$ | standard normal distribution function (the probit inverse link) and its inverse |

::: {#thm-ecological-norecovery}
## Aggregate meta-regression does not recover the individual effect-modifier coefficient
Let the individual-level model be probit, $\Phi^{-1}(\mu_t(x))=\eta_t(x)$, with arm-specific affine linear
predictors
$$
\eta_0(x)=a_0+\rho_0 x,\qquad \eta_1(x)=a_1+\rho_1 x ,
$$
so the individual-level effect-modification coefficient is $\beta_2=\rho_1-\rho_0$. Suppose each trial $j$
has a normal within-trial covariate distribution $X\sim\mathcal N(\bar x_j,\sigma^2)$ with a common
variance $\sigma^2$. Then the aggregate marginal contrast on the probit scale is an affine function of the
covariate mean,
$$
\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{1j})-\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{0j}) \;=\; c+b_2\,\bar x_j ,
$$ {#eq-limits-shrinkage}
with intercept and slope
$$
c=\frac{a_1}{\sqrt{1+\rho_1^2\sigma^2}}-\frac{a_0}{\sqrt{1+\rho_0^2\sigma^2}},
\qquad
b_2=\frac{\rho_1}{\sqrt{1+\rho_1^2\sigma^2}}-\frac{\rho_0}{\sqrt{1+\rho_0^2\sigma^2}} .
$$ {#eq-limits-b2}
The ecological slope $b_2$ equals the individual coefficient $\beta_2=\rho_1-\rho_0$ if and only if
$\sigma^2=0$ or $\rho_0=\rho_1$. Whenever $\sigma^2>0$ and $\rho_0\neq\rho_1$, the ecological slope is a
strict attenuation toward zero: $0<b_2<\beta_2$ if $\beta_2>0$, and $\beta_2<b_2<0$ if $\beta_2<0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @lem-limits-probit-integral with $Z=X\sim\mathcal N(\bar x_j,\sigma^2)$, $a=a_t$, $b=\rho_t$,
$$
\bar\mu_{tj}=\mathbb E[\Phi(a_t+\rho_t X)]=\Phi\!\left(\frac{a_t+\rho_t\bar x_j}{\sqrt{1+\rho_t^2\sigma^2}}\right),
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{tj})=\frac{a_t+\rho_t\bar x_j}{\sqrt{1+\rho_t^2\sigma^2}} ,
$$
applying $\Phi^{-1}$ to both sides. Differencing the arms,
$$
\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{1j})-\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{0j})
=\frac{a_1+\rho_1\bar x_j}{\sqrt{1+\rho_1^2\sigma^2}}-\frac{a_0+\rho_0\bar x_j}{\sqrt{1+\rho_0^2\sigma^2}}
=\underbrace{\Bigl(\tfrac{a_1}{\sqrt{1+\rho_1^2\sigma^2}}-\tfrac{a_0}{\sqrt{1+\rho_0^2\sigma^2}}\Bigr)}_{c}
+\underbrace{\Bigl(\tfrac{\rho_1}{\sqrt{1+\rho_1^2\sigma^2}}-\tfrac{\rho_0}{\sqrt{1+\rho_0^2\sigma^2}}\Bigr)}_{b_2}\bar x_j,
$$
which is @eq-limits-shrinkage with the coefficients @eq-limits-b2; the relationship is affine in $\bar x_j$
because $\sigma^2$ is common across trials.

Write $h(\rho)=\rho/\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}$, so that $b_2=h(\rho_1)-h(\rho_0)$ and $\beta_2=\rho_1-\rho_0$.
Differentiating by the quotient rule,
$$
h'(\rho)=\frac{\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}-\rho\cdot\frac{\rho\sigma^2}{\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}}}{1+\rho^2\sigma^2} .
$$
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}$ clears the inner fraction, and the
numerator becomes $(1+\rho^2\sigma^2)-\rho^2\sigma^2=1$, so
$$
h'(\rho)=\frac{(1+\rho^2\sigma^2)-\rho^2\sigma^2}{(1+\rho^2\sigma^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{1}{(1+\rho^2\sigma^2)^{3/2}} ,
$$
whence $0<h'(\rho)\le 1$ for all $\rho$, with $h'(\rho)=1$ only at $\rho=0$ (assuming $\sigma^2>0$). By the
fundamental theorem of calculus, for $\rho_1>\rho_0$,
$$
b_2=h(\rho_1)-h(\rho_0)=\int_{\rho_0}^{\rho_1}h'(\rho)\,d\rho .
$$
Since $0<h'(\rho)\le1$ with equality only on the single point $\rho=0$, the integrand is positive, giving
$b_2>0$; and it is strictly below $1$ except at that one point. A single point has Lebesgue measure zero,
so it does not affect the value of the integral, and therefore
$b_2<\int_{\rho_0}^{\rho_1}1\,d\rho=\rho_1-\rho_0=\beta_2$. Hence $0<b_2<\beta_2$ when $\beta_2>0$; the case
$\beta_2<0$ is identical with the inequalities reversed. If $\sigma^2=0$ then $h'(\rho)\equiv1$ and
$b_2=\rho_1-\rho_0=\beta_2$; if $\rho_0=\rho_1$ then $\beta_2=0$ and $b_2=h(\rho_0)-h(\rho_0)=0=\beta_2$.
These are the only equality cases. $\square$
:::

*Why this matters.* The slope @eq-limits-b2 is the ecological coefficient an analyst would obtain by
regressing the aggregate probit contrasts on the trial covariate means, and @thm-ecological-norecovery
shows it is a shrunk image of the true within-patient interaction $\beta_2$, with shrinkage controlled by
the within-trial spread $\sigma^2$. An analyst who reads the between-trial slope $b_2$ as the
effect-modification coefficient underestimates the modification, and so under-corrects the Bucher bias. We
put numbers on it before drawing the two general consequences.

::: {#exm-limits-probit-eco}
## Ecological attenuation of an effect-modifier coefficient
Take the probit model of @thm-ecological-norecovery with one covariate and parameters
$$
\alpha=-0.5,\quad \beta_1=0.8,\quad \gamma=0.4,\quad \beta_2=0.6,
$$
in the parameterization $\Phi^{-1}(\mu_t(x))=\alpha+\beta_1 x+(\gamma+\beta_2 x)t$, so the arm linear
predictors are $\eta_0(x)=-0.5+0.8x$ and $\eta_1(x)=-0.1+1.4x$, with slopes $\rho_0=0.8$ and
$\rho_1=\beta_1+\beta_2=1.4$. The individual-level effect-modification coefficient is $\beta_2=0.6$. Let the
common within-trial covariate variance be $\sigma^2=1$.

**Shrinkage factors.** From @eq-limits-b2,
$$
\sqrt{1+\rho_0^2\sigma^2}=\sqrt{1.64}=1.28062,\qquad \sqrt{1+\rho_1^2\sigma^2}=\sqrt{2.96}=1.72047 ,
$$
$$
h(\rho_0)=\frac{0.8}{1.28062}=0.62470,\qquad h(\rho_1)=\frac{1.4}{1.72047}=0.81373 .
$$

**Ecological coefficient.**
$$
b_2=h(\rho_1)-h(\rho_0)=0.81373-0.62470=0.18903 .
$$
An aggregate meta-regression would estimate the effect-modification coefficient as $0.189$, against the
true individual value $\beta_2=0.6$: an attenuation to about $31.5\%$ of its size. The ecological bias of
the coefficient is $b_2-\beta_2=0.189-0.600=-0.411$. These are the numbers that appear in the illustrative
table at the start of @sec-limits-ecological.

**Two trials, checked directly.** With intercepts $a_0=\alpha=-0.5$ and $a_1=\alpha+\gamma=-0.1$, a trial
with covariate mean $\bar x=0$ has
$$
\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_0)=\frac{-0.5}{1.28062}=-0.39044,\qquad \Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_1)=\frac{-0.1}{1.72047}=-0.05813,
$$
so its aggregate probit contrast is $-0.05813-(-0.39044)=0.33231$. A trial with $\bar x=1$ has
$$
\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_0)=\frac{0.3}{1.28062}=0.23426,\qquad \Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_1)=\frac{1.3}{1.72047}=0.75560,
$$
with contrast $0.75560-0.23426=0.52134$. The slope between the two trials is
$0.52134-0.33231=0.18903=b_2$, confirming @eq-limits-shrinkage.

**The Jensen gap, concretely.** At $\bar x=0$ the aggregate control-arm mean is
$\bar\mu_0=\Phi(-0.39044)=0.34811$, whereas the plug-in value is $\Phi(\eta_0(0))=\Phi(-0.5)=0.30854$. The
arm-level ecological bias is $\mathrm{EB}_0=0.30854-0.34811=-0.03957$ of @eq-ecological-bias: evaluating the
individual model at the mean covariate understates the true aggregate event probability by about four
percentage points.

**Against the average-conditional contrast.** The average-conditional contrast in a trial with mean
$\bar x$ is $\gamma+\beta_2\bar x=0.4+0.6\bar x$, with slope $0.6=\beta_2$ exactly. At $\bar x=0$ it is
$0.40$ versus the marginal $0.33231$, and at $\bar x=1$ it is $1.00$ versus the marginal $0.52134$. The
gap, $0.06769$ at $\bar x=0$ growing to $0.47866$ at $\bar x=1$, is the non-collapsibility gap, and its
growth is precisely what bends the marginal slope down from $0.60$ to $0.189$; @prp-limits-eco-noncollapse
below makes this identity exact. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Two consequences deserve emphasis, and the first is important enough to state as a proposition.

::: {#prp-limits-eco-noncollapse}
## Ecological bias and non-collapsibility are the same Jensen gap
In the probit model of @thm-ecological-norecovery, the average-conditional contrast in trial $j$ is affine
in $\bar x_j$ with slope exactly $\beta_2$, while the marginal (aggregate) contrast @eq-limits-shrinkage is
affine in $\bar x_j$ with the strictly smaller slope $b_2$. The difference between the two contrasts, in
each single population, is the non-collapsibility gap of @def-non-collapsibility; equivalently it is the
arm-differenced Jensen gap of @lem-limits-aggregation-jensen. Ecological bias of the coefficient
(@eq-limits-coef-eb) is thus non-collapsibility applied to the *slope* of the effect-modification function.
:::

::: {.proof}
By linearity of the linear predictor, the average-conditional contrast is
$$
\tilde d_{10(\mathcal P_j)}=\mathbb E_{f_j}[\eta_1(X)-\eta_0(X)]=(a_1-a_0)+(\rho_1-\rho_0)\bar x_j=\gamma+\beta_2\bar x_j,
$$
with $\gamma=a_1-a_0$, so its slope in $\bar x_j$ is $\beta_2$. The marginal contrast is
$\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{1j})-\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{0j})=c+b_2\bar x_j$ by @eq-limits-shrinkage, with $b_2<\beta_2$
by @thm-ecological-norecovery. Their difference in population $j$ is
$$
\bigl[\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{1j})-\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{0j})\bigr]-\tilde d_{10(\mathcal P_j)}
=\bigl[\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{1j})-\mathbb E_{f_j}\eta_1\bigr]-\bigl[\Phi^{-1}(\bar\mu_{0j})-\mathbb E_{f_j}\eta_0\bigr],
$$
and each bracket is, up to sign, the arm-level gap between $g$ applied to the aggregate mean and the
average of $g$ applied pointwise, that is the arm-level Jensen gap of @lem-limits-aggregation-jensen and
the non-collapsibility gap of @def-non-collapsibility for that arm. The contrast-level gap is their
difference, and since it equals $(c-\gamma)+(b_2-\beta_2)\bar x_j$, its slope in $\bar x_j$ is exactly the
coefficient-level ecological bias $b_2-\beta_2$ of @eq-limits-coef-eb. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Aggregate data do not carry the missing information.** The shrinkage depends on $\sigma^2$, the
within-trial variance of the covariate. If $\sigma^2$ varied across trials, @eq-limits-shrinkage would not
even be affine in $\bar x_j$, and no single ecological slope would exist. The dependence on a within-trial
moment that aggregate means do not report is the precise reason aggregate meta-regression cannot recover
$\beta_2$: the quantity it needs has been integrated away in forming the trial summaries. Only patient-level
data, where $\sigma^2$ and the individual interaction are both visible, restore it. This is the
information-theoretic core of why population adjustment requires IPD from at least one trial. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The constant term shows the same phenomenon.** @prp-limits-eco-noncollapse is about the slope; the
intercept tells the same story. When there is no effect modification, $\rho_0=\rho_1=\rho$ and
@eq-limits-b2 gives $b_2=0$ but $c=(a_1-a_0)/\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}=\gamma/\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}<\gamma$:
the marginal probit effect is strictly attenuated from the conditional effect $\gamma$ even with a constant
conditional contrast. That is non-collapsibility of the probit in its purest form, the intercept-level twin
of the surcharge illustration in @sec-limits-surcharge. Both the slope shrinkage and the intercept
shrinkage are instances of @lem-limits-aggregation-jensen for the nonlinear inverse link. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Reading the two failures side by side {#sec-limits-example}

The two worked examples, @exm-limits-bucher-rd and @exm-limits-probit-eco, are the two failures of this
chapter in miniature. Placing them side by side isolates what each one teaches and shows that they are two
faces of a single problem: an *averaging* done in the wrong place.

| Feature | Bucher failure (@exm-limits-bucher-rd) | Ecological failure (@exm-limits-probit-eco) |
|---|---|---|
| Scale | risk difference (directly collapsible) | probit (non-collapsible) |
| What breaks | an effect modifier is imbalanced across trials | the aggregate slope shrinks the interaction |
| Data assumed | conditional contrasts known | only trial means and trial contrasts |
| Symptom | indirect estimate has the wrong sign ($-0.01$ vs $+0.05$) | $b_2=0.189$ against $\beta_2=0.60$ |
| Root cause | the right contrast averaged over the wrong population | a nonlinear link averaged, destroying within-trial spread |
| Cure | reweight the contrast to $f_{*}$ | model IPD and integrate (Chapter 20) |

Both are averaging failures. The first averages the *correct* conditional contrast against the *wrong*
covariate distribution, so it is repaired by changing the distribution you average against (reweight to
$f_{*}$). The second destroys the conditional contrast by averaging through a nonlinear link *before*
differencing, so it is repaired by keeping the individual model and integrating it honestly. Population
adjustment does both at once: it estimates the conditional contrast from IPD and integrates it over the
target population. That is the subject of the next section and of Part IV.

## The gap that population adjustment fills {#sec-limits-gap}

The two failures of this chapter have a common diagnosis, and it is the diagnosis that defines Part IV.
Standard NMA fails because it **averages the wrong conditional effects over the wrong populations**: it
subtracts each trial's marginal effect, which is the trial's own conditional contrast averaged over the
trial's own covariate distribution, and neither the contrast nor the distribution is the one the target
estimand requires. Population-adjusted methods are needed because they estimate conditional effects and
average them over the *target* population.

The failure-of-Bucher theorem (@thm-failure-of-bucher) says that an unadjusted indirect comparison is
biased by $\int\tau^g_{AC}(f_{AC}-f_{*})-\int\tau^g_{BC}(f_{BC}-f_{*})$, and that the bias is removed by
re-expressing each trial's conditional contrast as an average against the *target* covariate distribution
$f_{*}$ rather than the trial's own. Two ingredients are needed to perform that re-expression: the
conditional contrast function $\tau^g_{tC}(\cdot)$, which is the effect-modification structure of the
treatment, and the target distribution $f_{*}$. The ecological-bias theorem (@thm-ecological-norecovery)
says that the first ingredient cannot be recovered from aggregate data alone, because aggregating a
nonlinear link over a covariate distribution destroys exactly the within-trial information that pins down
the interaction slope $\beta_2$. The remedy must therefore (i) estimate $\tau^g_{tC}(\cdot)$, and in
particular its effect-modification slope, from individual patient data in at least one trial, and (ii)
integrate the resulting individual model over the target covariate distribution, never substituting the
target mean into the individual model, since by @lem-limits-aggregation-jensen that substitution is itself
biased.

::: {.remark}
**What a valid indirect comparison must compute.** This is the checklist Part IV builds on.

1. **The conditional contrast function $\tau^g_{tC}(\cdot)$** (the effect-modification structure),
   estimated from individual patient data in at least one trial. Aggregate data cannot recover it
   (@thm-ecological-norecovery).
2. **The target covariate distribution $f_{*}$**, with the individual model integrated against it, never
   the target mean plugged into the model (@lem-limits-aggregation-jensen).

A method that supplies both closes the gap; a method that supplies neither is standard NMA. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The three methods of Part IV and Part V realize the two ingredients differently; each bullet ends with the
data it needs.

- **Matching-adjusted indirect comparison** (Chapter 18) reweights the IPD trial's individuals so that
  their weighted covariate moments match the aggregate trial's, then forms the contrast on the reweighted
  sample. The weights perform the integration against $f_{*}$ implicitly; the effective sample size
  (@thm-cauchy-schwarz-exp, the Cauchy-Schwarz bound on $(\sum w_i)^2/\sum w_i^2$) measures how much
  precision the reweighting costs. *Data needed:* IPD in one study and aggregate covariate moments in the
  target.
- **Simulated treatment comparison** (Chapter 19) fits the conditional outcome model $\mu_t(\cdot)$ on the
  IPD trial and then evaluates it at the aggregate trial's covariate distribution, integrating the model
  rather than plugging in the mean, which is the correct response to @lem-limits-aggregation-jensen. *Data
  needed:* an IPD-fitted outcome model plus the target covariate summaries or distribution.
- **Multilevel network meta-regression** (Chapter 20) writes the aggregate likelihood as the exact
  integral of the individual model over the within-study covariate distribution, $\bar\mu_{tj}=\int g^{-1}(\eta_t(x))f_j(x)\,dx$,
  the very integral of @eq-ecological-bias, and estimates the shared individual-level coefficients,
  including $\beta_2$, from the IPD and AgD studies jointly. It is the method that confronts the
  aggregation gap head on by computing it instead of ignoring it. *Data needed:* IPD and AgD modeled
  jointly, with the covariate distribution of every study.

Each method, in its own idiom, supplies the conditional contrast and the target integration that
@thm-failure-of-bucher and @thm-ecological-norecovery prove are necessary. That is the sense in which the
limits established in this chapter are not a dead end but a specification: they say exactly what a valid
indirect comparison must compute, and the rest of the book is the construction and analysis of methods
that compute it.

## Notes and references {#sec-limits-notes}

The failure-of-Bucher theorem and its bias decomposition @eq-limits-bias are result E.3 of the proof
catalogue (`proofs/E_population_adjustment_theory.md`); the development here expands the catalogue's
one-line argument into the full statement with the vanishing and genuineness clauses, and frames it as the
exact residual of @thm-bucher-unbiased when marginal constancy is weakened to conditional constancy. The
distinction between marginal and average-conditional relative effects, @def-conditional-marginal-contrast,
and the role of direct collapsibility in collapsing the two, follow the estimand-based account of
@chandler2026transport and the thesis of @phillippo2019thesis; the underlying collapsibility theory is
Chapters 7 and 11 (@def-non-collapsibility, @def-collapsibility, @thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr). The
mechanism that only imbalanced effect modifiers, not prognostic variables, bias an anchored comparison
(@cor-limits-pv-no-bias) is the anchored-cancellation result whose algebraic core is machine-checked in the
Coq development as `anchored_PV_cancellation` in `theories/EffectModifiers.v`; the same file's
`not_EM_does_not_imply_not_PV` underwrites the EM-versus-PV distinction of @thm-emcoll-em-pv-distinct used
here. The identification of conditional constancy with the shared effect modifier assumption of
@phillippo2016tsd18 is the bridge from the book's estimand language to the trial-methodology literature.

Ecological bias is the classical ecological fallacy of @phillippo2020mlnmr in the indirect-comparison
setting; the closed-form probit shrinkage @eq-limits-b2 is the Gaussian-integration identity that makes
multilevel network meta-regression analytically tractable for the probit link, and the general statement
that aggregating a nonlinear link is not the link of the aggregate is the motivation for ML-NMR's
integration step. The Gaussian probit integral @eq-limits-probit-integral is classical; the proof by an
auxiliary independent normal is the standard device. The reduction of both ecological bias and
non-collapsibility to a single Jensen gap (@thm-jensen) for the inverse link, promoted here to
@prp-limits-eco-noncollapse, is the unifying observation of this chapter, and it is the reason
@phillippo2016tsd18 treats covariate adjustment on the correct scale as the central methodological
requirement of a population-adjusted comparison. The definition of ecological bias (@def-ecological-bias)
is given here for the book; it specializes the epidemiological notion to the affine-linear-predictor
setting used throughout Parts IV and V.

The chapter owns the slugs `thm-failure-of-bucher` (catalogue E.3) and `def-ecological-bias` (new). The
pedagogical additions of this revision introduce the running example @exm-limits-psoriasis, the
binary-covariate special case @prp-limits-binary-bias with @eq-limits-binary-bias, the coefficient-level
ecological bias @eq-limits-coef-eb, and the unifying @prp-limits-eco-noncollapse; none renames an existing
label. The symbols $\tilde d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ (average-conditional effect) and
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$ (target average-conditional contrast) are used as in
@def-conditional-marginal-contrast and @eq-limits-target; they are proposed additions to the notation
chapter. The worked examples are self-contained and hand-verifiable; the probit example doubles as the
simplest exact instance of the integral that Chapter 20 computes numerically in general.

## Exercises {#sec-limits-exercises}

Exercises marked with a star ($\star$) have complete worked solutions in Appendix F. The first two are
warm-ups: do them before the computational and proof exercises that follow.

::: {#exr-limits-identify-em}
**(Warm-up.) Spotting the effect modifier.** Using the psoriasis stratum-risk table of
@exm-limits-psoriasis, (a) compute the two risk-difference contrasts $\tau_{AC}(x)=\mu_C(x)-\mu_A(x)$ and
$\tau_{BC}(x)=\mu_C(x)-\mu_B(x)$ in each stratum, and confirm which of $A$-versus-$C$ and $B$-versus-$C$ is
modified by prior exposure; (b) without computing the full bias, use the binary formula
@eq-limits-binary-bias and the fact that $p_{AC}=0.2<p_{*}=0.5$ to predict the *sign* of the Bucher bias;
(c) say in one sentence which trial's imbalance is harmless and why.
:::

::: {#exr-limits-interpret-se}
**(Interpretation.) A narrow interval is not a safe interval.** A colleague reports an indirect
$A$-versus-$B$ odds ratio of $1.08$ with a $95\%$ confidence interval of $(1.02,1.14)$ and concludes that
$B$ is worse than $A$. Explain, citing the mechanism of @thm-failure-of-bucher and the warning that the
standard error is silent, why this narrow interval does not establish that the point estimate is unbiased.
Name the one thing you would inspect to judge the risk of bias, and explain why, in the minimal anchored
triangle, you cannot instead test for it from the trial outcomes.
:::

::: {#exr-limits-recompute-bias}
**(Computation.) Recomputing a transitivity bias.** A binary effect modifier $X$ acts on the
$A$-versus-$C$ contrast on the risk-difference scale with conditional contrasts $\tau_{AC}(0)=0.05$ and
$\tau_{AC}(1)=0.35$, while the $B$-versus-$C$ contrast is unmodified at $\tau_{BC}\equiv0.10$. The
prevalences are $p_{AC}=0.3$, $p_{BC}=0.6$, and $p_{*}=0.5$. Compute the Bucher estimand, the target
contrast $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},\mathrm{id}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$, and the bias, and verify the bias
through the decomposition @eq-limits-bias and again through the binary formula @eq-limits-binary-bias. State
which contrast supplies the bias and why the imbalance in the other contrast is harmless.
:::

::: {#exr-limits-probit-recompute}
**(Computation.) Probit attenuation with a smaller spread.** Repeat the computation of
@exm-limits-probit-eco with within-trial variance $\sigma^2=0.25$ instead of $\sigma^2=1$, keeping all
other parameters. Compute the new ecological coefficient $b_2$ and the ecological bias $b_2-\beta_2$, and
verify that the attenuation is milder than at $\sigma^2=1$ but still present. Explain in one sentence why
$\sigma^2\to0$ recovers $\beta_2$ and why that limit is unattainable in any real trial.
:::

::: {#exr-limits-jensen-sign}
**(Computation.) Sign of the aggregation gap.** For the log link, $g(\mu)=\log\mu$ and
$g^{-1}(\eta)=e^{\eta}$, show that the arm-level ecological bias @eq-ecological-bias is always negative (the
plug-in arm mean understates the aggregate mean) for any non-degenerate covariate, and compute it exactly
when $\eta_t(X)$ is normal with mean $m$ and variance $v$. (Hint: $\mathbb E[e^{\eta}]=e^{m+v/2}$ by the
lognormal mean; compare with $e^{m}$.) Relate the multiplicative factor $e^{v/2}$ to the shrinkage factor
of @eq-limits-b2.
:::

::: {#exr-limits-zero-bias-trap}
**(Interpretation and proof.) A nonzero imbalance with zero bias.** Construct conditional contrasts
$\tau_{AC}(\cdot)$ on a binary covariate and prevalences $p_{AC}\neq p_{*}$ such that $X$ is a genuine
effect modifier of $A$ versus $C$ yet the contribution $b_{AC}$ in @eq-limits-bias is exactly zero. (Hint:
by @eq-limits-binary-bias, $b_{AC}=s_{AC}(p_{AC}-p_{*})$; a jump $s_{AC}\neq0$ can still give $b_{AC}=0$
only if the prevalence difference vanishes, so revisit the hint: instead make the two population *means* of
$\tau_{AC}$ coincide by a different route, using a covariate with more than two levels.) Explain why this
does not contradict @thm-failure-of-bucher(2), and connect your example to the distinction between a
class-wise and a contrast-wise necessity statement.
:::

::: {#exr-limits-logit-compound}
**(Challenge.) Compounding with non-collapsibility.** Reconsider @exm-limits-bucher-rd but report the
comparison on the logit (log odds-ratio) scale instead of the risk-difference scale, using the same stratum
risks. Compute each trial's *marginal* log odds-ratio
$d_{tC(\mathcal P_j)}=\operatorname{logit}(\bar\mu_t)-\operatorname{logit}(\bar\mu_C)$ from the marginalized
arm risks, the resulting Bucher estimand, and the target *average-conditional* log odds-ratio. Show that the
total discrepancy now exceeds the $-0.06$ of the risk-difference analysis, and identify the two additive
sources, the differential-effect-modification bias of @eq-limits-bias and the non-collapsibility gap of
@prp-limits-collapse-link(3). (Hint: compute the marginalized arm risks first, for example
$\bar\mu_C=(1-p)\mu_C(0)+p\,\mu_C(1)$ in each trial, then take logits; the surcharge illustration of
@sec-limits-surcharge is the same computation in miniature.)
:::

::: {#exr-limits-pv-cancellation}
**($\star$) (Proof.) Prognostic variables cancel, effect modifiers do not.** Let the covariate split as
$X=(V,W)$ with $V$ an effect modifier and $W$ purely prognostic for the anchored contrast on scale $g$, so
that $\tau^g_{tC}(v,w)=\tau^g_{tC}(v)$ does not depend on $w$. Suppose $\mathcal P_{AC}$, $\mathcal P_{BC}$,
and $\mathcal P^{*}$ have arbitrary, mutually different joint distributions of $(V,W)$. Prove from
@thm-failure-of-bucher that the Bucher bias depends only on the marginal distributions of $V$ across the
three populations and is invariant to every difference in the distribution of $W$, including differences in
the dependence between $V$ and $W$. Deduce that an anchored adjustment that balances $V$ alone is
sufficient, and state precisely where the argument would break for an unanchored comparison built from
absolute arm means rather than contrasts.
:::

::: {#exr-limits-general-attenuation}
**($\star$) (Challenge.) Monotone attenuation for a general link.** Let $g^{-1}$ be smooth and let each
trial have $X\sim\mathcal N(\bar x_j,\sigma^2)$ with common $\sigma^2$. Define the aggregate arm mean
$\bar\mu_t(\bar x)=\mathbb E[g^{-1}(a_t+\rho_t X)]$ as a function of the trial mean $\bar x$, and the
aggregate link-scale contrast $D(\bar x)=g(\bar\mu_1(\bar x))-g(\bar\mu_0(\bar x))$. Using a second-order
Taylor expansion of $g^{-1}$ in $\sigma^2$, show that the local ecological slope $D'(\bar x)$ equals the
individual coefficient $\beta_2=\rho_1-\rho_0$ to zeroth order in $\sigma^2$ and acquires an $O(\sigma^2)$
correction governed by the curvature $(g^{-1})''$ and the third derivative of $g^{-1}$. Specialize to the
probit and recover the leading-order term of @eq-limits-b2 by expanding $1/\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}$.
Comment on why a globally convex $g^{-1}$ does not guarantee attenuation toward zero for every parameter
configuration, in contrast to the exact probit result. (Hint: start from
$\bar\mu_t(\bar x)=g^{-1}(\eta_t(\bar x))+\tfrac12(g^{-1})''(\eta_t(\bar x))\rho_t^2\sigma^2+O(\sigma^4)$,
the Jensen gap of @lem-limits-aggregation-jensen to second order.)
:::
